 One week until midterm elections, early voting continues to outpace 2022 totals in North Carolina 
 By Michael Perchick Tuesday, October 27, 2026 10:47PM 
 NC voters are turning out in large numbers ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, with more than 1.773M ballots cast through Monday. RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- North Carolina voters are turning out in large numbers ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, with more than 1,773,889 ballots cast through Monday, about 37% more than at the same point in 2022.
 Wake County leads the state with more than 222,000 ballots cast. The county has 18 early voting sites this year, the most it has ever had for a midterm election.
 "We're seeing unprecedented turnout, which is amazing to see, especially in a midterm election. We have, for early voting, a 20% increase in number of sites and hours available to our voters. We're hoping that that played a part in this. People are coming out and voting, and it's just great to see," Wake County Board of Elections Director Olivia McCall said.
 Voters who spoke with ABC11 pointed to an array of issues motivating them to cast their ballots.
 "There's a lot of talk about housing, but nobody's really offering solutions. So trying to get new people to actually make some things happen," voter Pete Sack said.
 "The climate of the United States, something has to change. Gas prices, cost of living," voter Crystal Weeks said.
 "Taxes, the economy, (the) current administration," said voter Jeffrey Johnson.
 "We just moved here recently, about two months ago from New York, so taxes are a very big concern because we are pursuing a new ownership," said voter Arlene Blaize.
 Party registration figures show Democrats accounting for nearly 41% of ballots cast so far, followed by unaffiliated voters at just under 35% and Republicans at nearly 25%, according to State Board of Elections data.
 Black voters are also accounting for a larger share of ballots cast than their share of registered voters. They make up slightly more than 19% of registered voters in North Carolina but account for nearly 22% of ballots cast so far.
 Marcus Bass, Executive Director of the North Carolina Black Alliance, said voters are being driven by more than political affiliation.
 "(The higher turnout is a result of) the dissatisfaction that Black voters are seeing in government. The lack of investment in their priorities. And I think for a lot of us that are going into the ballot box this election cycle, it's not just about a political party," Bass said.
 Bass said the organization's outreach began before the March primaries and has continued for months, with attention extending beyond races at the top of the ballot.
 "I think it is very important to see that all voters, but more in particular Black voters, are seeing how important elections are in shaping the makeup of the courts. They're seeing the makeup of boards of education and the impact of investment, or lack thereof, in education," Bass said.
 He expects Black voter turnout to continue increasing through the closing days of early voting.
 "I think Black voter turnout as a whole, especially in these last couple of days for early voting, is going to continue to rise. And I think North Carolina is going to see a historic wave, even bigger than the 2008 numbers. Everybody always compares election turnout to black voters in 2008. We're a much larger state now. We have a lot larger voting share," Bass said.

 Hispanic voters are also showing increased participation compared with the previous midterm election.
 State Board of Elections data shows Hispanic voters make up nearly 4.7% of registered voters but account for slightly more than 3% of ballots cast so far. However, Catawba College Political Science Professor Dr. Michael Bitzer reports that roughly 3% share of in-person voting is more than double (1.3%) the rate at the same point in 2022.
 Nikki Mar í n Baena, co-director of Siembra NC, said the early participation is noteworthy.
 "In the past, sometimes Latinos are kind of Election Day voters, so this is also really exciting that people are voting early," Marin Baena said.
 Despite that increase, Marin Baena said she has seen candidates doing less outreach to Latino voters.
 "If anything, I would say that there's actually been a downshift in candidates meeting with the Latino community or doing information sessions in Spanish or collaborating with organizations like ours. We've actually seen less of that."
 Marin Baena said Latino voters are focused on issues affecting their families and daily lives.
 "I think because the Latino electorate, especially in a state like North Carolina, is a relatively new and young electorate, they are not that loyal to party, but they are looking at is real day-to-day issues, and so do people in their family feel safe. Do people in their family feel like they can afford groceries? Do people in their family feel like their power bill is too high and they don't understand why?" said Baena.
 According to Pew Research , compared to 2022, more Latino voters say they are extremely motivated to vote, while nearly twice as many more respondents say they have given a lot of thought to the upcoming elections.

 Early voting in North Carolina runs through 3 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31.
